topic: rebuilding a cart wheel: loose felloes, dry elm stock and refitting the iron tyre

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: wilgotnosciomierz (moisture gauge) na warsztacie

base: I am rebuilding the front wheel of my grandfather's cart and the felloes have worked loose.
An old barrow wheel hangs above the bench and its joints have never shifted at all.
A moisture gauge sits on the windowsill and I test the elm stock with it weekly.
The iron tyre still grips, though the spokes rattle when the cart crosses rough ground.
Should I cut a new felloe first, or take the tyre off before anything else?
Take the tyre off first, because every later measurement depends on the bare wheel sitting true.
A tyre under strain hides slack joints and you will fit the new felloe wrongly.
Once it is off, chalk the joints and see which ones open under light hand pressure.
Green elm shrinks for years, so a wheel built damp will loosen no matter how well cut.
I drew the tyre off cold with wedges and three of the felloe joints opened at once.
The moisture gauge reads fourteen percent on the old stock and nineteen on the plank I bought.
That barrow wheel above the bench must have been built from far drier timber.
Should I wait for the new plank to dry, or steam it and hope for the best?
Wait, because steaming softens the wood without taking any real moisture out of it.
Nineteen percent will give up another five in a warm shed over two or three months.
Stack it with laths between the boards and turn the pile once a fortnight.
Meanwhile cut the spokes to length, since dry spoke stock is easier to find than felloe stock.
The moisture gauge now reads fifteen percent on the plank and the pile stayed flat.
I cut two felloes and drove them onto the spokes, which went in tighter than expected.
The wheel now stands a little dished, rather more than the barrow wheel ever was.
Is that dish a fault, or does a cart wheel want some of it by design?
Dish is wanted, because the wheel must resist the sideways thrust of a loaded cart.
A barrow carries its load straight down, so that wheel needs almost none of it.
Half an inch across a four foot wheel is normal and will settle as the tyre goes on.
Measure the dish at every spoke and even out any that stand proud of the rest.
I evened the dish and the wheel now sits square when I spin it on the pin.
The old tyre, though, no longer meets round the rim and leaves a finger wide gap.
The smith says he can cut and weld it, but warns the wheel may end up smaller.
Is it better to shorten the old tyre, or have a new hoop rolled from flat bar?
Shorten the old one, since worn tyre iron is tougher than anything rolled today.
A finger wide gap costs you about an inch of circumference, which is nothing serious.
Have him weld it hot and dress the scarf down flush with a file afterwards.
Then measure the wheel and the hoop cold, and take the difference before any heating.
The welded hoop measures three eighths short of the wheel, which sounds about right to me.
We plan to heat it in a ring fire and drop it over the rim tomorrow.
I have a barrel of water ready, though I am unsure how fast to cool it.
Should the whole wheel go under, or only the tyre get the water?
Water the tyre only, running it round the rim so the iron cools evenly all through.
Dunking the whole wheel steams the joints open and undoes the work you have just done.
Two of you should pour steadily while a third keeps the wheel turning on the plate.
When the hissing stops, leave it a full day before you load the cart again.
